claim: Over the past several decades, a trend toward delayed childbirth has led to increases in parental age at the time of conception.
source: Over the past several decades, a trend toward delayed childbirth has led to increases in parental age at the time of conception.
evidence: This is a general statement about demographic trends that is presented as established fact in the introduction.

claim: Delayed parenthood is attributed to secular and socioeconomic factors.
source: This delayed parenthood is attributed to secular and socioeconomic factors (Waldenström, 2016), reproductive technological advancement (Bray et al., 2006), and higher levels of post-graduate education (Mills et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waldenström, 2016.

claim: Delayed parenthood is attributed to reproductive technological advancement.
source: This delayed parenthood is attributed to secular and socioeconomic factors (Waldenström, 2016), reproductive technological advancement (Bray et al., 2006), and higher levels of post-graduate education (Mills et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bray et al., 2006.

claim: Delayed parenthood is attributed to higher levels of post-graduate education.
source: This delayed parenthood is attributed to secular and socioeconomic factors (Waldenström, 2016), reproductive technological advancement (Bray et al., 2006), and higher levels of post-graduate education (Mills et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mills et al., 2011.

claim: The suppressive role of overpopulation on reproductive behavior was hypothesized.
source: The suppressive role of overpopulation on reproductive behavior was also hypothesized (Suvorov, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suvorov, 2021.

claim: Higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hassan and Killick, 2003.

claim: Higher male age is associated with lower odds of live birth.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horta et al., 2019.

claim: Higher male age is associated with adverse health of offspring in later life.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009.

claim: Higher male age is associated with increased susceptibility to early development of cancer in offspring.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Contreras et al., 2017.

claim: Higher male age is associated with increased risk of schizophrenia in offspring.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gratten et al., 2016.

claim: Higher male age is associated with increased risk of autism in offspring.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that higher male age contributes to poor pregnancy outcomes (Hassan and Killick, 2003), lower odds of live birth (Horta et al., 2019), and adverse health of offspring in later life (Montgomery et al., 2004; Puleo et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2009), including increased susceptibility to early development of cancer (Contreras et al., 2017), as well as neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Gratten et al., 2016) and autism (Reichenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reichenberg et al., 2006.

claim: Higher male age in mice is associated with reduced life span in offspring.
source: In experiments with mice it was demonstrated that higher male age is associated with reduced life span in offspring (Xie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2018.

claim: Advanced paternal age is linked with altered offspring phenotype via age-dependent changes in the sperm epigenome.
source: Increasing evidence links advanced paternal age with altered offspring phenotype via age-dependent changes in the sperm epigenome (Ashapkin et al., 2023; Jenkins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ashapkin et al., 2023; Jenkins et al., 2014.

claim: Age is a powerful factor affecting DNA methylation in mammalian sperm.
source: Published data indicate that age is a powerful factor affecting DNA methylation and other epigenetic markers in mammalian sperm (Ashapkin et al., 2023), and age-dependent changes in these epigenetic mechanisms are involved in the regulation of key developmental pathways, including nervous system-related signaling, Wnt, Hippo, mTOR, and Igf1 (Guo et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020; Pilsner et al., 2021; Suvorov et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2018; Yoshizaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ashapkin et al., 2023.

claim: Age-dependent changes in epigenetic mechanisms in sperm are involved in the regulation of key developmental pathways, including nervous system-related signaling, Wnt, Hippo, mTOR, and Igf1.
source: Published data indicate that age is a powerful factor affecting DNA methylation and other epigenetic markers in mammalian sperm (Ashapkin et al., 2023), and age-dependent changes in these epigenetic mechanisms are involved in the regulation of key developmental pathways, including nervous system-related signaling, Wnt, Hippo, mTOR, and Igf1 (Guo et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020; Pilsner et al., 2021; Suvorov et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2018; Yoshizaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020; Pilsner et al., 2021; Suvorov et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2018; Yoshizaki et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanistic link between age and epigenetic changes in sperm remains unknown.
source: Despite this evidence, the mechanistic link between age and epigenetic changes in sperm remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Final DNA methylation profiles of spermatozoa are a result of epigenetic events that occur during spermatogenesis.
source: Final DNA methylation profiles of spermatozoa are a result of epigenetic events that occur during spermatogenesis (Wu et al., 2015b), including meiotic divisions of spermatogonia and spermatocytes associated with passive loss of methylation and de novo methylation (Oakes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2015b and Oakes et al., 2007.

claim: Global methylation drop of around 12–13% occurs in preleptotene spermatocytes.
source: Global methylation drop of around 12–13% occurs in preleptotene spermatocytes and methylation is gradually reestablished during leptotene-pachytene stages so that the final DNA methylation patterns are obtained by the end of pachytene spermatocyte stage (Gaysinskaya et al., 2018; Loukinov et al., 2002; Oakes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaysinskaya et al., 2018; Loukinov et al., 2002; Oakes et al., 2007.

claim: Methylation is gradually reestablished during leptotene-pachytene stages so that the final DNA methylation patterns are obtained by the end of pachytene spermatocyte stage.
source: Global methylation drop of around 12–13% occurs in preleptotene spermatocytes and methylation is gradually reestablished during leptotene-pachytene stages so that the final DNA methylation patterns are obtained by the end of pachytene spermatocyte stage (Gaysinskaya et al., 2018; Loukinov et al., 2002; Oakes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaysinskaya et al., 2018; Loukinov et al., 2002; Oakes et al., 2007.

claim: The transition from elongating spermatids to late spermatids is associated with changes in methylation of more than 5000 DNA regions in rats.
source: A recent rat study identified the transition from elongating spermatids to late spermatids as another stage associated with changes in methylation of more than 5000 DNA regions (El Omri-Charai et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to El Omri-Charai et al., 2023.

claim: After fertilization, most parental-specific epigenetic marks of gametes undergo reprogramming to establish totipotency in the developing embryo.
source: After fertilization, most parental-specific epigenetic marks of gametes undergo reprogramming to establish totipotency in the developing embryo.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about epigenetic reprogramming.

claim: Imprinted loci, certain classes of repetitive sequences, and other genomic loci escape epigenetic reprogramming after fertilization.
source: However, imprinted loci, certain classes of repetitive sequences, and other genomic loci escape this reprogramming event and contribute to a non-Mendelian form of inheritance as demonstrated in humans (Atsem et al., 2016; Denomme et al., 2020) and rodents (Oluwayiose et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2018), suggesting that the final sperm epigenome acquired during spermatogenesis is a significant channel for the transfer of inheritable information to the next generation (Lismer and Kimmins, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atsem et al., 2016; Denomme et al., 2020; Oluwayiose et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2018.

claim: The final sperm epigenome acquired during spermatogenesis is a significant channel for the transfer of inheritable information to the next generation.
source: However, imprinted loci, certain classes of repetitive sequences, and other genomic loci escape this reprogramming event and contribute to a non-Mendelian form of inheritance as demonstrated in humans (Atsem et al., 2016; Denomme et al., 2020) and rodents (Oluwayiose et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2018), suggesting that the final sperm epigenome acquired during spermatogenesis is a significant channel for the transfer of inheritable information to the next generation (Lismer and Kimmins, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lismer and Kimmins, 2023 and inference from previous citations.

claim: Epigenetic events during spermatogenesis occur in the unique biochemical environment of the apical compartment of seminiferous epithelium, protected from body fluids by the blood-testis barrier (BTB).
source: Epigenetic events during spermatogenesis occur in the unique biochemical environment of the apical compartment of seminiferous epithelium, protected from body fluids by the blood-testis barrier (BTB) – the tightest blood-tissue barrier composed of coexisting tight junctions, basal ectoplasmic specializations, gap junctions, and desmosomes in Sertoli cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The BTB is the tightest blood-tissue barrier composed of coexisting tight junctions, basal ectoplasmic specializations, gap junctions, and desmosomes in Sertoli cells.
source: Epigenetic events during spermatogenesis occur in the unique biochemical environment of the apical compartment of seminiferous epithelium, protected from body fluids by the blood-testis barrier (BTB) – the tightest blood-tissue barrier composed of coexisting tight junctions, basal ectoplasmic specializations, gap junctions, and desmosomes in Sertoli cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The BTB regulates the entry of chemical compounds, including nutrients, hormones, electrolytes, and harmful toxicants, thus creating a unique and highly selective environment for germ cells undergoing epigenetic reprogramming.
source: The BTB regulates the entry of chemical compounds, including nutrients, hormones, electrolytes, and harmful toxicants, thus creating a unique and highly selective environment for germ cells undergoing epigenetic reprogramming (Mok et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mok et al., 2013a.

claim: In rodents, age-dependent declines in fertility are caused by deterioration of the BTB.
source: In rodents, age-dependent declines in fertility are caused by deterioration of the BTB (Levy et al., 1999; Paul and Robaire, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levy et al., 1999; Paul and Robaire, 2013.

claim: BTB integrity is determined by the balance between activities of the two complexes of mTOR in Sertoli cells.
source: Recent studies demonstrate that BTB integrity is determined by the balance between activities of the two complexes of the serine/threonine kinase mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) in Sertoli cells, whereby mTOR complex one (mTORC1) promotes disassembly of the BTB and mTOR complex two (mTORC2) promotes its integrity (Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a; Mok et al., 2013a; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: mTORC1 promotes disassembly of the BTB.
source: Recent studies demonstrate that BTB integrity is determined by the balance between activities of the two complexes of the serine/threonine kinase mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) in Sertoli cells, whereby mTOR complex one (mTORC1) promotes disassembly of the BTB and mTOR complex two (mTORC2) promotes its integrity (Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a; Mok et al., 2013a; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: mTORC2 promotes BTB integrity.
source: Recent studies demonstrate that BTB integrity is determined by the balance between activities of the two complexes of the serine/threonine kinase mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) in Sertoli cells, whereby mTOR complex one (mTORC1) promotes disassembly of the BTB and mTOR complex two (mTORC2) promotes its integrity (Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a; Mok et al., 2013a; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Cheng, 2016; Mok et al., 2013a, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: mTOR expression is highest in testes out of all tissues in humans.
source: mTOR expression is highest in testes out of all tissues in humans (Fagerberg et al., 2014) and mice (Yue et al., 2014), and the mTOR pathway is recognized today as a major mechanism of longevity and aging regulation (Papadopoli et al., 2019; Weichhart, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fagerberg et al., 2014.

claim: mTOR expression is highest in testes out of all tissues in mice.
source: mTOR expression is highest in testes out of all tissues in humans (Fagerberg et al., 2014) and mice (Yue et al., 2014), and the mTOR pathway is recognized today as a major mechanism of longevity and aging regulation (Papadopoli et al., 2019; Weichhart, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yue et al., 2014.

claim: The mTOR pathway is recognized as a major mechanism of longevity and aging regulation.
source: mTOR expression is highest in testes out of all tissues in humans (Fagerberg et al., 2014) and mice (Yue et al., 2014), and the mTOR pathway is recognized today as a major mechanism of longevity and aging regulation (Papadopoli et al., 2019; Weichhart, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Papadopoli et al., 2019; Weichhart, 2018.

claim: Only two clusters of CpG methylation patterns were significantly enriched representing linear increase and linear decrease in methylation over the entire analyzed age-period (56-334 PND).
source: STEM analysis demonstrated that only two clusters were enriched significantly representing linear increase and linear decrease in methylation over the entire analyzed age-period (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis using STEM and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within the studied period (56–334 PND), methylation of most DNA regions undergoing age-dependent changes in methylation in sperm is associated with age linearly or semi-linearly.
source: These results suggest that within the studied period (56–334 PND), methylation of most DNA regions undergoing age-dependent changes in methylation in sperm is associated with age linearly or semi-linearly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the STEM analysis results showing only linear patterns.

claim: Staining of Sertoli cells with Raptor antibodies was abolished in Rptor KO animals.
source: Indeed, staining of Sertoli cells with Raptor and Rictor antibodies was abolished in corresponding KO animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Staining of Sertoli cells with Rictor antibodies was abolished in Rictor KO animals.
source: Indeed, staining of Sertoli cells with Raptor and Rictor antibodies was abolished in corresponding KO animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In mice with suppressed mTORC2 the BTB was loose enough to allow biotin to migrate to the lumen of seminiferous tubules.
source: As predicted, in mice with suppressed mTORC2 the BTB was loose enough to allow biotin to migrate to the lumen of seminiferous tubules (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by biotin tracer assay shown in Figure 4.

claim: 1731 age-dependent DMRs were identified in the mTORC1 experiment.
source: Using this approach, we identified 1731 age-dependent DMRs in the mTORC1 experiment and 797 DMRs in the mTORC2 experiment, with 79 common DMRs identified in both experiments.
evidence: Based on RRBS data analysis comparing 8- and 22-week-old WT mice.

claim: 797 age-dependent DMRs were identified in the mTORC2 experiment.
source: Using this approach, we identified 1731 age-dependent DMRs in the mTORC1 experiment and 797 DMRs in the mTORC2 experiment, with 79 common DMRs identified in both experiments.
evidence: Based on RRBS data analysis comparing 8- and 22-week-old WT mice.

claim: 79 common DMRs were identified in both mTORC1 and mTORC2 experiments.
source: Using this approach, we identified 1731 age-dependent DMRs in the mTORC1 experiment and 797 DMRs in the mTORC2 experiment, with 79 common DMRs identified in both experiments.
evidence: Based on RRBS data analysis comparing 8- and 22-week-old WT mice.

claim: In both experiments age-dependent changes were dominated by an age-dependent increase in methylation.
source: In both experiments age-dependent changes were dominated by an age-dependent increase in methylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 based on RRBS data.

claim: Lists of genes associated with significant age-dependent DMRs are enriched with developmental categories in both experiments.
source: This analysis demonstrated that in both experiments, lists of genes associated with significant age-dependent DMRs are enriched with developmental categories (Figure 5A and B), indicative of the possibility that age-dependent changes in sperm DNA methylation may be causative of the transfer of different developmental epigenetic information to the next generation.
evidence: Based on Metascape enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Common highly enriched categories across both experiments included tube morphogenesis, brain development, cell morphogenesis, and other categories relevant to growth, embryo development, development of nervous system, muscles, and others.
source: Specifically, common highly enriched categories across both experiments included tube morphogenesis, brain development, cell morphogenesis, and other categories relevant to growth, embryo development, development of nervous system, muscles, and others.
evidence: Based on Metascape enrichment analysis of age-dependent DMRs.

claim: Enriched molecular mechanisms were dominated by small GTPase-mediated signal transduction and regulation of kinase activity.
source: Enriched molecular mechanisms were dominated by small GTPase-mediated signal transduction and regulation of kinase activity (protein phosphorylation, signaling by receptor tyrosine kinase, and other).
evidence: Based on Metascape enrichment analysis of age-dependent DMRs.

claim: 2738 significant DMRs were induced by mTORC1 inactivation in mature mice.
source: We identified 2738 significant DMRs induced by mTORC1 inactivation in mature mice (Amir et al., 2023) and compared them with age-dependent DMRs in WT animals.
evidence: Based on RRBS data analysis comparing WT and Rptor KO mice at 22 weeks.

claim: Most of the DNA regions induced by genetic manipulation of Raptor undergo hypomethylation – the direction of change opposite to the one induced by age.
source: Most of the DNA regions induced by genetic manipulation of Raptor undergo hypomethylation – the direction of change opposite to the one induced by age (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on RRBS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Age-dependent and mTORC1 KO-dependent DMR lists were highly overlapping with p<0.00001.
source: According to this analysis the two lists were highly overlapping with p<0.00001, indicative that age and mTORC1 inactivation in Sertoli cells affect the similar sets of DMRs in sperm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation (r = –0.48, p=2.1e–14) between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC1 inactivation.
source: We observed a strong negative correlation between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC1 inactivation (r = –0.48, p=2.1e–14), suggesting that in mature animals, mTORC1 inactivation in Sertoli cells returns age-dependent DMRs to their younger state.
evidence: Based on Pearson correlation analysis of overlapping DMRs.

claim: In mature animals, mTORC1 inactivation in Sertoli cells returns age-dependent DMRs to their younger state.
source: We observed a strong negative correlation between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC1 inactivation (r = –0.48, p=2.1e–14), suggesting that in mature animals, mTORC1 inactivation in Sertoli cells returns age-dependent DMRs to their younger state.
evidence: This is an inference from the negative correlation between age and mTORC1 KO effects.

claim: The correlation between age and mTORC1 KO effects was even higher for DMRs that undergo 10% or higher change (r=–0.68, p=2.3e–4).
source: The correlation was even higher for DMRs that undergo 10% or higher change in relation to age or genetic manipulation (r=–0.68, p=2.3e–4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1632 significant DMRs were induced by decreased mTORC2 activity in Sertoli cells of young mice.
source: We identified 1632 significant DMRs induced by decreased mTORC2 activity in Sertoli cells of young mice (Amir et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on RRBS data analysis comparing WT and Rictor KO mice at 8 weeks.

claim: The majority of the DNA regions with methylation changes induced by genetic manipulation of Rictor undergo hypermethylation – the direction of change concordant with accelerated sperm aging.
source: The majority of the DNA regions with methylation changes induced by genetic manipulation of Rictor undergo hypermethylation – the direction of change concordant with accelerated sperm aging (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on RRBS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Age-dependent and mTORC2 KO-dependent DMR lists were highly overlapping with p<0.00001.
source: According to this analysis the two lists were highly overlapping with p<0.00001, indicative that age and mTORC2 inactivation in Sertoli cells affect the similar sets of DMRs in sperm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation (r=0.81, p<2.2e–16) between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC2 inactivation.
source: We observed a strong positive correlation between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC2 inactivation (r=0.81, p<2.2e–16), suggesting that in young animals, mTORC2 inactivation in Sertoli cells accelerates epigenetic aging of sperm.
evidence: Based on Pearson correlation analysis of overlapping DMRs.

claim: In young animals, mTORC2 inactivation in Sertoli cells accelerates epigenetic aging of sperm.
source: We observed a strong positive correlation between methylation changes induced by age and changes induced by mTORC2 inactivation (r=0.81, p<2.2e–16), suggesting that in young animals, mTORC2 inactivation in Sertoli cells accelerates epigenetic aging of sperm.
evidence: This is an inference from the positive correlation between age and mTORC2 KO effects.

claim: The correlation between age and mTORC2 KO effects was even higher for DMRs that undergo 10% or higher change (r=0.83, p<2.6e–8).
source: The correlation was even higher for DMRs that undergo 10% or higher change in relation to age or genetic manipulation (r=0.83, p<2.6e–8, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lists of genes associated with significant KO-dependent DMRs were enriched with developmental categories in both mTORC1 and mTORC2 experiments.
source: Given our data demonstrate that DNA methylation changes induced by suppression of mTOR complexes affect age-dependent genes in sperm, it is not surprising that in both experiments (mTORC1 and mTORC2 suppression) the lists of genes associated with significant KO-dependent DMRs were enriched with developmental categories (Figure 5C and D), indicative that age-dependent changes in mTOR pathway and in the BTB permeability may be causative of the transfer of altered developmental epigenetic information to the next generation.
evidence: Based on Metascape enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Enriched categories common for both mTORC1 and mTORC2 experiments included brain development, heart development, chordate embryonic development, pattern specification process, cell morphogenesis, muscle structure development, signaling by receptor tyrosine kinases, skeletal system development, sensory organ development, behavior, and protein phosphorylation.
source: Specifically, enriched categories common for both experiments included brain development, heart development, chordate embryonic development, pattern specification process, cell morphogenesis, muscle structure development, signaling by receptor tyrosine kinases, skeletal system development, sensory organ development, behavior, and protein phosphorylation.
evidence: Based on Metascape enrichment analysis of KO-dependent DMRs.

claim: Testes weight decreases with age in humans and laboratory rodents.
source: It was demonstrated previously that testes weight and sperm counts decrease with age, while the percent of morphologically abnormal spermatozoa increases with age in humans and laboratory rodents (Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016.

claim: Sperm counts decrease with age in humans and laboratory rodents.
source: It was demonstrated previously that testes weight and sperm counts decrease with age, while the percent of morphologically abnormal spermatozoa increases with age in humans and laboratory rodents (Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016.

claim: The percent of morphologically abnormal spermatozoa increases with age in humans and laboratory rodents.
source: It was demonstrated previously that testes weight and sperm counts decrease with age, while the percent of morphologically abnormal spermatozoa increases with age in humans and laboratory rodents (Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bujan et al., 1988; Gunes et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondria DNA copy number (mtDNAcn) increases with age in human sperm.
source: Additionally, mitochondria DNA copy number (mtDNAcn) increases with age in human sperm (Zhang et al., 2016) and it was shown recently that sperm mtDNAcn is a novel biomarker of male fecundity (Rosati et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Sperm mtDNAcn is a novel biomarker of male fecundity.
source: Additionally, mitochondria DNA copy number (mtDNAcn) increases with age in human sperm (Zhang et al., 2016) and it was shown recently that sperm mtDNAcn is a novel biomarker of male fecundity (Rosati et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rosati et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Mice with inactivated mTORC2 demonstrated significant decreases in testis weight.
source: Concordant with our hypothesis, mice with inactivated mTORC2 (permanently 'leaky' BTB) demonstrated significant decreases in testis weight and sperm counts concomitant with increase in morphologically abnormal sperm and mtDNAcn (Table 1; Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6A.

claim: Mice with inactivated mTORC2 demonstrated significant decreases in sperm counts.
source: Concordant with our hypothesis, mice with inactivated mTORC2 (permanently 'leaky' BTB) demonstrated significant decreases in testis weight and sperm counts concomitant with increase in morphologically abnormal sperm and mtDNAcn (Table 1; Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6B.

claim: Mice with inactivated mTORC2 demonstrated increase in morphologically abnormal sperm.
source: Concordant with our hypothesis, mice with inactivated mTORC2 (permanently 'leaky' BTB) demonstrated significant decreases in testis weight and sperm counts concomitant with increase in morphologically abnormal sperm and mtDNAcn (Table 1; Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6C.

claim: Mice with inactivated mTORC2 demonstrated increase in mtDNAcn.
source: Concordant with our hypothesis, mice with inactivated mTORC2 (permanently 'leaky' BTB) demonstrated significant decreases in testis weight and sperm counts concomitant with increase in morphologically abnormal sperm and mtDNAcn (Table 1; Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6D.

claim: Inactivation of mTORC1 resulted in testes weight decrease.
source: Inactivation of mTORC1 resulted in testes weight decrease and slight increase in mtDNAcn but did not affect sperm parameters significantly.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6A.

claim: Inactivation of mTORC1 resulted in slight increase in mtDNAcn.
source: Inactivation of mTORC1 resulted in testes weight decrease and slight increase in mtDNAcn but did not affect sperm parameters significantly.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6D.

claim: Inactivation of mTORC1 did not affect sperm parameters significantly.
source: Inactivation of mTORC1 resulted in testes weight decrease and slight increase in mtDNAcn but did not affect sperm parameters significantly.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 6B-C.

claim: Mice with inactivated mTORC2 in Sertoli cells have a reproductive phenotype concordant with accelerated aging.
source: These results suggest that although permanent changes of the mTOR complexes balance in either direction may have negative consequences for some reproductive parameters, mice with inactivated mTORC2 in Sertoli cells have a reproductive phenotype concordant with accelerated aging.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed reproductive parameters in Rictor KO mice.

claim: The balance of mTOR complexes in Sertoli cells regulates the rate of sperm epigenetic aging.
source: These results demonstrate for the first time that the balance of mTOR complexes in Sertoli cells regulates the rate of sperm epigenetic aging.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental results.

claim: mTOR pathway in Sertoli cells may be used as a novel target of therapeutic interventions to rejuvenate the sperm epigenome in advanced-age fathers.
source: Thus, mTOR pathway in Sertoli cells may be used as a novel target of therapeutic interventions to rejuvenate the sperm epigenome in advanced-age fathers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: The sperm epigenome responds to a broad range of factors, including paternal diet.
source: An accumulating body of literature indicates that the sperm epigenome responds to a broad range of factors, including paternal diet (Watkins et al., 2018), physical activity (Benito et al., 2018), stress (Wu et al., 2016), metabolic status (Donkin et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2014), and environmental exposures (Wu et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Watkins et al., 2018.

claim: The sperm epigenome responds to physical activity.
source: An accumulating body of literature indicates that the sperm epigenome responds to a broad range of factors, including paternal diet (Watkins et al., 2018), physical activity (Benito et al., 2018), stress (Wu et al., 2016), metabolic status (Donkin et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2014), and environmental exposures (Wu et al., 2017), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Benito et al., 2018.

claim: The hypothesis that epigenetic aging of sperm results from the loss of BTB integrity requires additional research to test.
source: Given that BTB is responsible for the maintenance of a unique biochemical environment for germ cells undergoing DNA methylation changes (Gaysinskaya et al., 2018; Loukinov et al., 2002; Oakes et al., 2007; El Omri-Charai et al., 2023) and its permeability increases with age (Levy et al., 1999; Paul and Robaire, 2013), these facts taken together provide a strong basis for a hypothesis that epigenetic aging of sperm results from the loss of BTB integrity. Additionally, research is needed to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the integration of multiple findings.

claim: 56 weeks of age in mice is equivalent to advanced paternal age in humans.
